passage: The sceptic's argument has an irritating simplicity. You claim to know that you are sitting in a room reading. But if you were dreaming vividly, or if your experiences were being produced by some elaborate deception, everything would seem exactly as it now does. Since you cannot tell from the inside that you are not in such a situation, you cannot rule it out; and if you cannot rule it out, the sceptic concludes, you do not know that you are reading. The argument generalises to almost everything, and many careful attempts to refute it have the air of a lawyer winning on a technicality rather than of anyone actually seeing the truth.

One response is to concede the argument and shrug: perhaps we know nothing, but we must act as if we did, and so nothing of practical importance changes. This concession is too generous. It treats the sceptic's standard, that knowing requires excluding every alternative one cannot distinguish from the actual situation, as if it were simply the correct standard, which we happen to fall short of. Yet we nowhere apply that standard outside the philosophy seminar. A birdwatcher who reports a heron on the riverbank is not asked whether she has excluded the possibility of a mechanical decoy indistinguishable at that distance; she is asked whether she looked carefully, knows her birds and had a clear view. If a park ranger has just announced that decoys have been placed along that stretch of river, the question changes, and it is right that it should.

What this suggests is that the alternatives a knower must exclude are fixed by something other than bare conceivability: by what is live in the circumstances, by what a reasonable person has some ground to take seriously. The sceptic does not discover a hidden flaw in our ordinary claims; he changes the subject by importing a standard that no ordinary claim was ever meant to satisfy. This is why his argument feels at once unanswerable and beside the point.

None of this makes scepticism worthless. Its exaggerated standard has the merit of exposing how much of our confidence rests on background assumptions we rarely state, and in particular circumstances, the decoy case among them, those assumptions deserve scrutiny. The error lies in moving from the observation that every assumption could in principle be questioned to the conclusion that every assumption must be questioned before anything is known. The first is a useful reminder; the second would make knowledge impossible by definition, and a definition that guarantees its own emptiness is a poor account of what we were trying to describe.

options.B: she could not tell from the inside whether she was dreaming the scene she reported to others.
options.C: someone in a position to know had just announced that decoys were placed along that part of the river.
options.D: her view of the riverbank had been partly blocked by trees or by the light on the water.

passage: Intellectual humility is praised more often than it is defined, and the praise tends to blur it with other things. Sometimes it is equated with low confidence, as if the humble thinker were one who held every opinion loosely. Sometimes it is identified with deference, the willingness to yield to those who know more. And sometimes it means no more than a modest manner, the habit of prefacing one's claims with 'I may be wrong, but'. Each of these captures something, yet none of them can be the virtue itself, because each can be present where humility is absent and absent where humility is present.

Take low confidence first. A person may be unsure of everything out of sheer timidity, believing too little rather than too much, and timidity of this kind is no more admirable than arrogance; it is merely a different way of misjudging one's evidence. Conversely, someone may be entirely certain that the earth orbits the sun, and rightly so, without any failure of humility. Deference fares no better. It is often wise, but a thinker who deferred to every apparent authority would be credulous rather than humble, and one who refused to defer to a genuine expert on a question outside her competence might be guilty of several faults without its being clear that humility is the one she lacks. As for the modest manner, it concerns how one presents oneself to others, and it can coexist with a private conviction that one is never mistaken. The phrase 'I may be wrong' is cheap to say.

A more promising account locates humility in a person's relation to her own limitations. The humble thinker is one who notices the gaps in her knowledge, the places where her reasoning is shaky and the biases to which she is prone, and who takes these into account: she seeks out the evidence she lacks, rechecks the steps she is unsure of, and discounts the conclusions she has special reason to want. This is compatible with great confidence where her grounds are good. Indeed, it is partly because she is alert to where her grounds are poor that her confidence elsewhere deserves to be taken seriously. Her humility, on this view, is not a feeling about herself but a settled pattern of attention and correction, visible chiefly in what she does whenever her own judgement is at stake.

It may be objected that this account makes humility indistinguishable from good reasoning in general. Anyone who reasons well, after all, attends to the strength of her evidence. But the two can come apart. A scientist may be superb at weighing evidence about the world and yet curiously blind to the ways in which her own ambitions shape which questions she asks and which results she finds convincing. Her failure is not a failure to reason about stars or cells; it is a failure to treat herself as one more possible source of error. That reflexive attention, directed at the reasoner rather than at the subject matter, is what the word humility usefully picks out.

The account has a further merit: it explains why humility can be overdone. A person preoccupied with her own limitations, forever cataloguing the ways in which she might be mistaken, may become unable to act on what she knows or to contribute what she has to offer. Owning one's limitations includes keeping them in proportion, and the thinker who is paralysed by self-scrutiny has misjudged them as surely as the one who ignores them.

passage: National accounts were designed to measure what passes through markets, and for most of their history they have counted the meal bought in a restaurant but not the meal cooked at home, the hour a paid nurse spends with an elderly patient but not the hour a daughter spends with her mother. The omission was never a secret: early statisticians acknowledged it and set it aside as a practical matter, since household work was hard to observe and there was no price at which to record it. The result, however, was a picture of the economy in which a large share of the work that keeps people alive appeared to be no work at all.

In recent decades, time-use surveys, in which people record how they spend each part of a day, have made it possible to estimate how many hours households devote to cooking, cleaning and care. Turning those hours into money, however, requires a choice between methods that rest on different assumptions. One method, replacement cost, asks what it would cost to hire someone to do the same tasks. Another, opportunity cost, asks what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment during those hours. The two methods can produce very different totals, and they can rank the same work differently: an hour of childcare by a surgeon is worth a great deal on the second method and rather little on the first.

Critics sometimes take this disagreement as proof that the whole exercise is arbitrary, but that conclusion is too quick. Every figure in national accounts rests on conventions, and the fact that a convention must be chosen does not make zero, the convention long in use, the neutral one. Recording household care at zero is also a valuation, and almost certainly the least accurate available. Estimates, even rough ones, have changed how policy debates can be conducted: they make it harder to describe cuts to public care services as savings when the work has simply moved into homes.

There is, nonetheless, a limit to what a price can capture. Both methods treat care as a bundle of tasks that could in principle be handed to someone else. Much of it can be. But part of what a family member provides is the fact that it is they who provide it, and that element has no market equivalent because it cannot be bought. A figure for unpaid care is therefore best understood as a floor rather than a measure: it shows that the work is not nothing, without claiming to say what it is worth.

options.B: the wage that would have to be paid to someone hired to carry out the same tasks.
options.C: what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment in that hour.
options.D: the price of the nearest service that can be bought, such as a meal eaten in a restaurant.

passage: A durable genre of business writing proceeds by a method that looks, at first sight, impeccably empirical. The author selects a number of companies that have performed outstandingly over a long period, studies them closely, and identifies the practices they share: a strong culture, perhaps, or a fierce attention to customers, or a willingness to abandon unprofitable lines. These practices are then offered as the causes of greatness, and the reader who adopts them is invited to expect something of the same result. The books sell well, partly because the companies are vivid and partly because the method appears to replace opinion with evidence.

The first difficulty is one of selection. By studying only the companies that succeeded, the method has no way of knowing how many companies followed the same practices and failed. If a great many firms had strong cultures and attended closely to their customers, and most of them disappeared, then these traits are not what separated the winners from the rest; they were simply common, and the winners, being a subset of the many, happened to possess them as well. The graveyard of failed firms is not consulted because it cannot easily be visited: failed companies leave few records, attract no researchers and give no interviews.

A second difficulty is subtler. Many of the traits that the method identifies are not observed independently of performance but described after the fact, by people who already know the result. A company that is doing well is said to have a bold strategy and a confident leadership; the same company, a few years later and in decline, is said to have been reckless and arrogant, though nothing in its conduct may have changed. The observers are not being dishonest when they do this; they are reading the same conduct in the light of what it later led to. Where descriptions of this kind are the raw material, the correlation between good practices and good results is partly manufactured by the way in which the practices were recognised.

Defenders of the genre have an answer to the first point: compare the successful firms with a matched set of less successful ones, drawn from the same industries and periods. This is a real improvement and should be acknowledged as such. But it does not remove the second difficulty, since the comparison firms are still described by people who know how they fared, nor does it settle a third, which emerges only with time. Several of the companies held up as models in such studies later stumbled badly, and the explanation usually offered is that they abandoned the principles that had made them great. That explanation can be given whatever happens. A theory that accounts for success by the presence of certain practices, and for failure by their supposed absence, has arranged never to be wrong.

None of this shows that the study of successful firms is worthless. Close accounts of how particular companies work can suggest hypotheses worth testing, and some of the practices they describe may well be beneficial. What the genre cannot do is what it most often claims to do: to identify, from the records of the winners, the reasons they won. A reader who wishes to learn from such books would do better to treat their lists of principles as questions rather than answers, and to remember that in a competitive market a large part of any outcome may be owed to timing and circumstance, which no one can copy.

passage: Suppose a painting has hung for decades in a museum, admired by critics and loved by visitors, and is then shown beyond doubt to be a forgery. Nothing about the canvas has changed: its colours and its composition are exactly as they were, and the pleasure that thousands took in it was genuine pleasure, not a misunderstanding awaiting correction. Yet the picture is taken down, its value collapses, and the critics who praised it are embarrassed. If what matters in a painting is what can be seen in it, this reaction looks irrational, a triumph of the label over the eye.

Two familiar explanations are offered, and neither is adequate. The first says the reaction is mere snobbery: we cared about the famous name, not the picture, and the forgery has simply exposed the fact. There is truth here, since much of the fall in price reflects nothing loftier than the loss of a signature that could be resold. But the explanation proves too much; it implies that anyone who minds about the difference is a snob, including the scrupulous historian with no money at stake. The second says that the forgery must differ visibly after all, and that trained eyes, once alerted, can see its deadness. Sometimes this is so; yet the deadness is usually perceived only after the verdict is known, and a theory that can detect a difference only once it has been told where to look is not much of a theory.

A more promising account begins from the thought that we value paintings not only as arrangements of colour but also as achievements. To admire a picture fully is partly to admire what was done in making it: a problem of light or space confronted at a particular moment, with the means then available, by someone who did not know how it would turn out. The forger faces a different problem, that of producing something that will pass as the solution to the first. The two canvases may look alike, but they answer different questions, and the exposure tells us that the question we thought we were admiring an answer to was never asked by this canvas at all.

This view has a cost, and it should be admitted. It makes part of a painting's value depend on facts that cannot be seen in it, and so concedes that looking alone can never be the whole of appreciation. It also allows that a forgery may be a considerable achievement of its own kind, as a feat of imitation, without ranking it beside what it imitates. But the cost seems worth paying, because the alternative is to hold that the history of art could be rewritten, without loss, by anyone with a sufficiently skilful hand.

options.B: cast doubt on the second explanation by pointing out that the supposed visible flaws are noticed only after exposure.
options.C: introduce the author's own account, which holds that forgeries can always be distinguished by close study.
options.D: support the second explanation by showing that trained eyes can find the deadness of a forgery once they are alerted.

passage: Quantum theory is among the most precisely confirmed bodies of physics ever constructed, and it is also, by the admission of many who use it, a theory that does not quite say what it is about. The difficulty is usually called the measurement problem. The theory's central equation describes a system by a mathematical object, the wave function, which evolves smoothly and predictably for as long as nobody looks. Under that evolution a particle can come to be in a combination, or superposition, of possibilities: here and there, spinning one way and the other. Yet whenever an experimenter checks, the apparatus records exactly one result. The textbook rule bridges the gap by decree: at the moment of measurement the wave function 'collapses' to one of the possibilities, with probabilities that the theory supplies.

The trouble is that the rule invokes a notion the theory never defines. A measuring device is made of atoms, and atoms obey the smooth equation; treated as part of the physical system, the device should itself enter a superposition of having recorded each result, rather than recording one. Somewhere between the particle and the experimenter's notebook the smooth evolution is supposed to give way to the abrupt one, but the theory does not say where, or why, or what counts as a measurement in the first place. In practice nothing hangs on the answer, because the boundary can be drawn anywhere convenient without altering the predicted statistics. That is precisely what makes the problem so easy to ignore.

The proposed solutions divide, roughly, by what they are prepared to give up. Some modify the smooth equation, adding a tiny spontaneous tendency to collapse that is negligible for single particles but overwhelming for anything as large as a pointer. Others leave the equation untouched and deny that collapse ever happens: every possible outcome is realised, each in a branch of reality that cannot interact with the others, and the appearance of a single result is simply what being in one branch is like. Still others add a further ingredient to the wave function, definite positions for particles at all times, guided by the wave, so that the outcome was settled all along. A widely discussed physical process, in which a system's entanglement with its surroundings rapidly suppresses the signs of superposition, is often offered as a solution in its own right; it explains why superpositions of large objects are never seen, but on most accounts it does not explain why one outcome occurs rather than another.

Because these rival pictures agree, in nearly every experiment so far performed, with each other and with the textbook rule, a common response is to call the dispute metaphysics, a matter of taste for people who have finished their calculations. The response is understandable but confused. It treats the textbook rule as a neutral baseline from which the interpretations depart, when the rule is itself an interpretation, and an incomplete one, since it relies on a word it cannot define. Nor are the rivals strictly equivalent: the theories that modify the equation predict small departures from standard behaviour in sufficiently large systems, and experiments of increasing delicacy are now searching for them.

None of this obliges the working physicist to choose a side before computing a reaction rate; the theory's practical success is real, and it does not wait on the outcome of the debate. But a theory that works without our knowing what it describes has not thereby been shown to need no description. The measurement problem is not a puzzle from philosophy grafted onto physics. It is a gap in the statement of the physics itself, one that the theory's very success has made easy to step around.

options.A: explain why a gap in the theory's foundations makes so little difference to how the theory is used.
options.B: support the claim that rival interpretations differ in their predictions only for sufficiently large systems.
options.C: suggest that measuring devices, unlike the particles they record, do not obey the smooth equation of the theory.
options.D: show that the measurement problem has in effect been solved, since the location of the boundary makes no difference.

passage: When a welfare benefit goes unclaimed by many of the people entitled to it, the usual explanation is that they did not know about it, did not need it badly enough or could not be bothered. The explanation locates the problem in the claimant. It rarely asks what claiming actually involves: discovering that the benefit exists, working out whether one qualifies, gathering documents that may be held by three different offices, completing a form whose questions assume a settled address and a regular income, and then, often, doing it all again a few months later to prove that nothing has changed.

These demands are usually described as administrative friction, an unfortunate but neutral by-product of running any large programme. They are not neutral. Every hour required to claim is an hour that some people can spare more easily than others, and the people least able to spare it are frequently those the programme was meant to help: the seriously ill, those working irregular shifts, those for whom scarcity has already consumed much of the attention that form-filling demands. A requirement that costs a comfortable applicant an afternoon may cost a struggling one the benefit itself.

There is a further reason to look closely at such burdens. Because they are set through forms, procedures and office hours rather than through legislation, they can change who receives a benefit without any public decision that it should. A government that wished to spend less on a programme but did not wish to say so could add a document to the list or shorten the period for renewal, and the number of recipients would fall while the rules of entitlement stayed exactly as they were. Whether or not anyone intends this, the effect is a form of policy made out of sight, insulated from the debate that a change in the law would provoke.

This is not to say that verification is illegitimate. Public programmes depend on the belief that money goes to those entitled to it, and some checking sustains that belief among the taxpayers who fund them. But the costs of checking are borne in two places, in the office and in the lives of applicants, and only the first tends to be counted. A sound design would weigh the time and strain imposed on claimants as seriously as the cost of the errors it prevents, and would treat a large gap between entitlement and receipt as evidence about the system rather than about the people outside it.

options.C: overlooks the demands that the process of claiming itself places on the people entitled to the benefit.

passage: For much of its short history as a subject of research, the wandering mind was treated as noise. Participants in experiments were supposed to attend to the task in front of them, and the moments when their thoughts drifted to lunch or to an argument with a sibling were lapses to be minimised or averaged away. When researchers began to study these lapses directly, by interrupting people at random moments in their day and asking what they had been thinking about, the first surprise was how common the lapses were. The method had the merit of catching thought in the act, before the thinker had time to tidy it into a more respectable account of where her attention had been. A considerable part of waking thought, it turned out, is about something other than what the thinker is doing.

Two quite different interpretations of this finding have since competed. On the first, mind wandering is a failure of control: it is associated with errors in reading and driving, with poorer performance on tests of sustained attention and, in some studies, with lower reported mood at the moment of wandering. The mind that drifts is the mind that has lost its grip, and the remedy is training in attention. On the second interpretation, these costs are real but partial, and they ignore what the drifting mind is actually doing. Much wandering thought is directed at the future, at plans, rehearsals of conversations and the weighing of unfinished business, and some of the solutions that arrive unbidden in the shower or on a walk may owe something to the same process. On this view the mind that drifts is not idle but working on a different problem, one it has judged, so to speak, more pressing than the task at hand.

Each interpretation, I think, makes the same mistake, which is to speak of mind wandering as though it were one thing with one value. The evidence for costs comes largely from tasks that demand continuous attention, where any lapse is damaging by design, while the evidence for benefits comes largely from situations in which the external task is undemanding, so that little is lost by leaving it. Tasks of the first kind are chosen precisely because they make lapses easy to count, and situations of the second kind because they leave room for thought. It is hardly surprising that the two literatures reach different verdicts, since they are, for the most part, looking at different occasions. Nor does the link with low mood settle the matter. A person who is worried is likely both to feel worse and to find his thoughts pulled towards his worries, so that wandering may be as much a symptom of unhappiness as its cause.

A more useful question is not whether the mind should wander but when, and with what awareness. Drifting during a lecture one has chosen to attend is a cost; drifting while washing dishes may be a free opportunity to think. There also seems to be a real difference between thought that slips away unnoticed and thought that is allowed to roam, as when a person deliberately sets a problem aside and lets her attention go where it will. The second kind is under a loose but genuine control, since the person can notice it and call it back. If this is right, the goal of training attention should not be to abolish wandering, an aim that is probably unachievable and possibly harmful, but to make wandering more visible to the wanderer, so that she can tell which kind of occasion she is in.

passage: A piece of folk wisdom, repeated in many places, holds that a family business rarely survives the founder's grandchildren. The founder builds it through hard work, the children keep it going out of duty, and the grandchildren, raised in comfort, let it slip away. The story is usually told as a lesson about character: wealth softens those who inherit it, and the hunger that built the firm cannot be handed down along with the shares. It is a satisfying story, and like most satisfying stories it is only partly true.

Consider first the plain arithmetic of inheritance. A founder typically owns the whole firm and answers to no one. If the shares are divided among three children, and each of them divides theirs among three more, the third generation may consist of nine or more owners, some of whom work in the business and some of whom have never set foot in it. Those who draw a salary want the profits reinvested; those who live elsewhere want dividends; those who need cash want to sell, and there may be no agreed price at which the others can buy them out. Quarrels follow, but they follow from the structure, and the most energetic cousin in the world could not make them disappear.

A second difficulty lies in how leaders are chosen. A firm that insists the chief executive must be a member of the family has narrowed its field of candidates to a handful of people who happen to share a surname. Even if every one of them is capable, the chance that the best available manager is among them is small. The founder often makes matters worse by postponing the question altogether, because the business is so bound up with his sense of who he is that planning for his own departure feels like planning for his death. When the moment can no longer be avoided, it tends to arrive suddenly, through illness or a quarrel, and the successor is whoever is standing nearest.

None of this means that character is irrelevant; some heirs are indeed less driven than their parents, and some fortunes really are spent rather than lost. But the family firms that last for many generations tend to have one thing in common, and it is not a lucky supply of hard-working grandchildren. They separate the role of owner from the role of manager, write down rules for how shares may be sold within the family, and are willing to hire an outsider to run the business when no relative is suited to it. Their survival is less a triumph of virtue than of design.

passage: When people settle an argument about a word by 'looking it up', they treat the dictionary as a court whose ruling ends the case. The image is understandable, since a dictionary speaks in the flat, confident voice of a statute, but it misrepresents how the better dictionaries are made. A serious dictionary does not decide what words mean; it reports, as carefully and as comprehensively as it can, what speakers and writers have been observed to mean by them.

The method is easiest to see in the large historical dictionaries begun in the nineteenth century. Their editors did not sit down and define words from their own sense of correctness. They gathered evidence: slips of paper, many of them sent in by volunteer readers, on each of which a sentence containing a word had been copied out with its source and date. A definition was written only after the slips for a word had been sorted into piles according to the senses they seemed to show. Where the evidence was thin, the entry was thin; where a sense appeared in the slips before anyone had thought to approve of it, it went in regardless. The definition, on this model, is a summary of a body of quotations, and the quotations printed beneath it are not decoration but the grounds on which it rests.

It does not follow that a dictionary is a neutral mirror. The evidence has to be collected by someone, and collectors read some kinds of text more than others; for a long time published literary prose was heavily over-represented, while the speech of the street and the workshop barely appeared. Someone must also decide where one sense ends and another begins, a judgment the slips cannot make for themselves. And the labels a dictionary attaches, such as 'informal', 'nonstandard' or 'archaic', are themselves verdicts, even when they are offered as descriptions. A dictionary that claimed to have no point of view would simply be concealing the one it has.

The honest position lies between the court and the mirror. A good dictionary is an argument from evidence: its claims can be checked against the citations, and they can be revised when new evidence arrives, which is why the best dictionaries are never finished. To read one well is to notice the quotations as well as the definitions, and to treat its authority as that of a careful witness rather than a judge. That is a more modest authority than the one we usually grant it, but it is a sturdier one, since it does not collapse the first time usage moves on.

passage: It has become a commonplace that printing fixed the text. Before the press, the argument goes, every copy of a work was made by hand, and every copyist introduced errors of his own, so that texts drifted further from their originals with each generation of transcription. The press ended the drift: it produced hundreds of identical copies at once, and it was this identity, more than mere abundance, that allowed scholars across a continent to cite the same page and to dispute the same words. The thesis is powerful, and in its broad outline it is not wrong. But it credits the machine with an achievement that took centuries and required far more than machinery.

Look closely at the books of the hand-press period and the identical copies begin to dissolve. Printers corrected errors while a sheet was being run, stopping the press to change a letter or a line and then carrying on; the sheets already printed were too costly to waste and were bound up alongside the corrected ones. Two copies of the same edition may therefore differ on any number of pages, and it is possible that no surviving copy matches any other exactly. Reprints, authorised or not, introduced fresh errors and silent improvements of their own. To a reader of the period, a printed book was a more dependable object than a manuscript, but it was not the guaranteed replica that the commonplace imagines.

What made print seem fixed, then, was less the press than a slowly assembled set of expectations and institutions around it. Legal rights over copies gave publishers a motive to suppress unauthorised versions. Scholarly editors developed procedures for collating copies and establishing a single authoritative text. Readers learned to expect that a citation to page and line would lead others to the same words, and that expectation, once widespread, pressed printers toward the consistency it presupposed. Fixity was in this sense a social achievement that the technology made possible but did not by itself deliver.

The distinction matters because the same commonplace is now being run in reverse. Digital texts, we are told, are inherently unstable: they can be altered silently, updated without notice, made to differ from one reader's screen to the next. That is true of the technology, but the history of print suggests that it is not the whole story. Whether digital texts become stable will depend on whether comparable institutions grow up around them: archives that preserve versions, conventions for citing them, and readers who expect, and demand, that a text once published remains what it was. The machine sets limits; it does not settle the outcome.

passage: The demonstration is by now familiar. Two groups are offered the same choice, described in two ways: a treatment that leaves ninety in a hundred patients alive after a year, or one that sees ten in a hundred die. The numbers are identical, yet the first description reliably attracts more support than the second. Since the options do not differ, the argument runs, a rational agent should not respond to the difference in wording, and the fact that people do respond is evidence that their preferences are shaped by presentation rather than substance. The principle appealed to, that logically equivalent descriptions should produce the same choice, has seemed so obvious that few have thought it needed defending.

Yet the principle is less obvious than it looks once we remember that descriptions do not fall from the sky. Somebody chooses them, and the choice is rarely arbitrary. A doctor who believes a treatment is worth trying tends, without any intent to manipulate, to speak of the patients it saves; a doctor with doubts more naturally mentions those it fails. Speakers also tend to describe a quantity in terms of the reference point from which it has moved: a glass that was full and has been partly drunk is more often called half empty than half full. If such regularities hold, then the frame carries information that the bare numbers do not, and a listener who draws an inference from it is not being swayed by mere wording. She is reading what the speaker's choice of words reveals, much as she would read an emphasis or a pause.

On this view, many framing effects are better described as sensitivity to implicit information than as failures of logic, and the experimenter who insists on equivalence has mistaken the logic of sentences for the logic of conversation. The equivalence holds between the propositions; it does not hold between the acts of uttering them, because those acts tell the hearer different things about the speaker. Participants who bring their ordinary conversational competence into the laboratory are, in a sense, being too reasonable for the experiment's purposes.

This rehabilitation should not be pushed too far. When experiments go to some lengths to make the frame visibly arbitrary, for example by assigning descriptions by an evident coin toss or by presenting both descriptions together, the inference from frame to speaker has nothing to work on, and a rational participant should set it aside. Effects in such conditions are often smaller, which is what the information account predicts, but they do not always vanish. Some residue seems to reflect the plain pull of words such as 'die' and 'lose', a reaction that would survive any amount of reflection about speakers. The information account explains a good deal of the phenomenon; it does not explain all of it.

What follows is a more discriminating verdict than either side usually offers. Whether responsiveness to a frame is a lapse depends on whether, in the situation at hand, the frame was a signal. Outside the laboratory it usually is, which is why habits formed in conversation are worth having. The danger lies precisely in that usefulness. A listener who reasonably treats frames as informative can be exploited by a speaker who knows the convention and chooses a frame to suggest a recommendation he would not dare to state outright. The fault in such cases lies less with the listener's inference than with the speaker's abuse of a norm that ordinarily makes the inference sound.

passage: Two stories are told about the anger that seems to pervade online discussion, and each is convenient for someone. In the first, the ranking systems that decide what appears in a feed have manufactured outrage, turning otherwise reasonable people into combatants. In the second, told chiefly by those who build such systems, a feed merely reflects its users: it shows people what they engage with, and if what they engage with is furious, the fault lies in human nature, not in the code. The first story flatters users, who become the victims of a machine; the second flatters engineers, who become the neutral servants of a public. Neither is quite right.

Against the first story, it must be granted that outrage is old. Pamphleteers, broadsheets and street-corner orators discovered long before any computer that indignation sells, and audiences have always lingered over a scandal longer than over the correction that followed it. A ranking system that favours whatever holds attention did not invent this appetite. It found the appetite already there, and it could hardly have succeeded so quickly if it had not. Any account that treats the present climate as wholly unprecedented must therefore explain why the appetite it deplores appears so reliably in the commercial history of every earlier medium of mass communication.

But the second story trades on an ambiguity in the word 'want'. A feed ranked by engagement learns what people react to: what they click, what they pause over, what they reply to in anger. Reaction is not the same as endorsement. A person may linger over a provocative post in the way a driver slows to look at an accident, and may say, if asked afterwards, that she wishes she had seen less of such material. A system that learns only from the lingering will give her more of it, and will describe the result as giving her what she wants. It is giving her what she wanted in the moment of reaction, which may be the opposite of what she wants on reflection.

The older media of indignation differed in a further way that the mirror story overlooks. A newspaper editor chose what to print, but the feedback that reached him was slow and coarse, a matter of sales figures and letters to the editor. A feed reports, to every person who publishes in it, exactly how each post performed, often within minutes. Those who write for such an audience learn quickly which tone is rewarded, and many adjust accordingly, not because they are cynical but because they would like to be read. The ranking system therefore does not merely distribute a fixed supply of anger; it shapes the supply, by teaching producers what pays. A mirror that trains the face in front of it is not a mirror.

It does not follow that the remedy is simply to rank posts by what people say, on reflection, that they value. Reflective preferences are harder to measure, easier to misreport and, when a platform infers them, open to the charge that the platform has substituted its own judgement for the user's. These are real objections, and they counsel modesty about any redesign. But they cut both ways. A system that optimises for momentary reaction has also made a judgement about what its users really want; it has simply made that judgement silently, and in favour of the version of the user that is easiest to count. Neutrality, in this domain, is not an available option; the only choice is between an explicit conception of the user's interests and an implicit one.

options.B: defending the builders of ranking systems against critics who blame them for a feature of human nature.

passage: The idea that some jobs require workers to manage their own feelings, and not merely their hands or their minds, has travelled a long way from its origins in the study of flight attendants and debt collectors. It now turns up in discussions of nursing, teaching, retail and call centres, and even of the unpaid work of keeping a family cheerful. This expansion has drawn a predictable objection: if every job involves some management of emotion, the critics say, then the concept marks out nothing in particular. A surgeon must stay calm, a lawyer must appear confident, and a builder who loses his temper with clients will not keep them; are these, too, emotional labourers?

The objection is fair against the loose use of the term, but it misses what the original idea was pointing at. The distinction was never between jobs that involve feeling and jobs that do not. It was between feeling that a worker manages according to her own judgement and feeling whose display is specified, monitored and sold by someone else. The surgeon's calm serves the operation and is left to her; nobody scripts it. The call-centre agent, by contrast, may be told how often to use the customer's name, scored on the warmth of her voice, and disciplined for a sigh. The emotion is part of the product, and the employer, not the worker, sets its terms.

Seen this way, the concept is narrower than its popular use suggests, but also sharper. It directs attention not to the presence of emotion at work but to its ownership, and it suggests where the cost of such work lies. Most people can smile at a stranger without harm; the difficulty arises when the smile must be produced on demand, for hours, regardless of how the worker is treated, and when failing to produce it is a disciplinary matter. One would expect work of this kind to produce a fatigue unlike ordinary tiredness, and perhaps an uncertainty about which friendly feelings are one's own.

None of this implies that friendliness in service is a sham, or that customers who enjoy it are dupes. Many workers take pride in easing a stranger's day, and a scripted greeting can be delivered with real goodwill. The point is that goodwill freely given and goodwill required by contract are different things, even when they look identical from the other side of the counter, and a concept that cannot tell them apart has lost the very thing that made it worth having.

passage: As tariffs have fallen over the past several decades, attention in trade disputes has shifted to a less visible kind of obstacle: the technical standards a product must meet before it can be sold. Rules on labelling, safety testing, permitted additives and packaging are written for reasons that sound unimpeachable, and many of them are exactly what they claim to be. But a rule can protect consumers and domestic producers at the same time, and it is not always easy to say which purpose is doing the work.

The usual complaint is that standards are protectionism by other means, and examples are easy to imagine. Suppose a country requires that cheese be aged in wooden barrels of a particular kind, a method its own dairies have used for generations, while foreign producers age theirs in steel vessels that yield a product no less safe. The rule says nothing explicit about origin, and its authors need never mention foreign cheese at all, yet its effect is almost that of a ban on imports. A tariff of this severity would be denounced at once; dressed as a quality rule, it may pass unnoticed for years.

It does not follow, however, that every standard which burdens importers is suspect. Almost any rule imposes costs on foreign firms, if only because they must learn it, and societies differ honestly in the risks they will tolerate. One country may accept a pesticide residue that another refuses, not because its farmers lobbied but because its citizens weigh the balance between price and caution differently. To treat all such divergence as disguised protection would be to deny countries the right to set their own levels of acceptable risk, which is a large part of what self-government means.

The more useful test is therefore not whether a standard falls harder on foreigners, but whether its burden is necessary to the purpose it states. A rule that specifies an outcome, such as a maximum level of bacteria, leaves producers free to reach it by any method and so admits anyone who can meet it. A rule that specifies a method, when other methods would achieve the same outcome, deserves closer scrutiny, because the extra cost it imposes buys no additional safety. The distinction will not settle every dispute; outcomes can be hard to measure, and a method is sometimes prescribed precisely because checking the outcome is impractical. But it shifts the argument from motives, which are hard to prove, to fit, which can at least be examined.

passage: Early researchers in artificial intelligence expected to begin with the easy problems and work up to the hard ones. They took easy to mean what people find easy and hard to mean what people find hard, and so they assumed that a machine which could play respectable chess or prove theorems in logic would soon be able to fold laundry or cross a cluttered room. Matters turned out almost the other way round. Programs that could beat strong players at board games arrived long before machines that could reliably pick up an unfamiliar object without crushing or dropping it. The observation that the faculties we think of as higher are the cheap ones to mechanise, while those we take for granted are expensive, has come to be described by roboticists as a paradox.

It is a paradox only if our sense of difficulty is a good guide to the difficulty of a task, and a plausible explanation is that it is not. Perception and movement have been refined over an immense evolutionary history, and they run beneath awareness, so they feel like nothing at all. Explicit reasoning is recent and effortful, and its effortfulness is precisely what we notice. The feeling of difficulty, on this account, measures how new a skill is to our species rather than how much computation it requires.

The implication for work is uncomfortable for a familiar way of ranking jobs. We tend to treat the skills of the hospital cleaner, the gardener and the care worker as basic and those of the clerk who reconciles accounts as advanced. Yet the cleaner moves through rooms that are never arranged twice in the same way and handles objects of every shape and texture, while the reconciliation follows rules that can be written down. A machine finds the second job far easier to take over than the first. Forecasts that expect automation to climb steadily upward from the bottom of the wage scale may therefore have the direction partly backwards.

Two cautions are in order. First, the paradox describes a stage of technology, not a law of nature; methods that learn from vast numbers of examples have already eroded some of the advantage that perception once enjoyed, and it would be rash to assume the boundary will stay where it is. Second, being hard to automate is not the same as being well rewarded. The skills that resist machines are often widely shared among people, and abundance keeps wages low whatever a robot can or cannot do. The paradox tells us which tasks machines will struggle with; it does not tell us that the people who perform them will prosper.

passage: In the language of property, home and ownership have become almost interchangeable. To own the place one lives in is to 'have a home'; to rent is to be on the way to one, or to have failed to arrive. The equation is so familiar that it seems less a claim than a definition, and policies built on it, from subsidised mortgages to the sale of public housing to its tenants, present themselves not as choices among ways of housing people but as the extension of home itself to those who lack it.

Yet if one asks what people mean when they say that a place feels like home, the answers rarely mention title. They mention routines that have settled into the rooms, objects arranged by one's own hand, the confidence that one will be there next year, the freedom to decide who comes in, the ability to paint a wall or plant a window box or keep a dog. Home, in this sense, is less a thing one possesses than something one does, a practice of shaping a space and being shaped by it over time. And a practice of this kind needs two conditions: enough control over the space to shape it, and enough security of tenure to make the shaping worthwhile.

Neither condition is the same as ownership, though ownership has usually supplied both. A tenant on a twelve-month lease who may be asked to leave at short notice, who must seek permission to hang a picture, and whose rent can rise without limit, has good reason not to invest himself in his rooms; he is camping, however long he stays. But the cause of his condition is not that he rents. It is that his tenancy is short, revocable and hedged with prohibitions. Where tenancies are long, rents predictable and tenants free to alter their surroundings within reason, renters make homes much as owners do, while an owner whose mortgage payments consume most of his income, and who fears that a lost job means a lost house, may know the very precariousness that the equation reserves for tenants.

None of this means that ownership confers nothing distinctive. The owner can knock down a wall, not merely paint it; he can leave the house to his children; he answers to no landlord. A tenant, however secure, lives in a space whose final shape is decided by someone else. These are real goods, and it would be odd to deny that many people want them for good reasons. The objection is not to ownership but to the assumption that it is the only door into home, an assumption that directs public effort towards turning tenants into owners while leaving the conditions of tenancy, under which a large and often growing share of urban households live, largely untouched.

The cost of that assumption is not only sentimental. A household that expects to move at a landlord's word does not join the school committee, does not plant a tree it will not see grow, does not learn the names of neighbours it may lose within the year. Schools, associations and local shops all depend on residents who expect to stay long enough for their efforts to bear fruit. The practices through which people make a home are continuous with those through which they make a neighbourhood, so that insecurity inside the door becomes thinness of attachment outside it. To treat home as a matter of title is therefore to misunderstand not only what renters lack but what cities lose when they lack it.

passage: The mirror test has an appealing simplicity: an animal is given a mark it cannot see directly, perhaps a spot of odourless dye on the forehead, and is then shown a mirror. If it uses the reflection to inspect or rub at the mark on its own body, it is said to recognise itself. Great apes generally pass, most monkeys generally fail, and over the decades a handful of other species have been reported to pass or nearly pass. Because the result is so easy to state, it has come to be treated as a kind of membership test: those who pass belong among the self-aware, and those who fail are presumed to lack a self worth the name.

The test does measure something real. To pass, an animal must grasp that the moving figure in the glass is not another individual and that what it sees there corresponds to its own body. That is not a trivial achievement, and it is reasonable to think that animals capable of it have some representation of their own bodies as objects among others. The difficulty lies in what is inferred from failure, and in how much is read into success.

Consider failure first, since the test presupposes an animal that relies heavily on vision, that attends to its own appearance, and that is bothered enough by an odd mark to investigate it. Many animals meet none of these conditions. A dog, which navigates its world largely by smell, may simply have no interest in a silent image that gives off no scent; an animal whose species does not groom may see no reason to touch a spot on its skin. Failing a test designed around one animal's priorities is weak evidence that another animal lacks the capacity being tested, in the way that a person's failure to answer a question asked in an unfamiliar language reveals little about her knowledge.

Success is open to over-reading too. Recognising one's body in a mirror shows an understanding of the body as one's own; it does not show, by itself, that the animal reflects on its past, imagines its future or thinks of itself as a person with a history. These are richer capacities, and the leap from the mirror to them is a leap of interpretation, not of evidence. None of this makes the test worthless. It makes it one probe among many, informative within its range and silent outside it. The error is not in running the test but in letting a single, visually biased procedure decide which minds are admitted to the category of the self-aware.

passage: A randomised trial, for all its authority, answers a question about groups. It tells us that among patients like those enrolled, the people given a treatment did better on average than the people who were not, by an amount that can be estimated with known uncertainty. The doctor in a consulting room faces a different question, about a single person, and the gap between the two questions has produced two opposite errors, each of which presents itself as wisdom.

The first error is to apply the average as though it were a fact about each patient. If a drug lowers the risk of a stroke over five years from ten in a hundred to seven in a hundred, it is tempting to say that it reduces every patient's risk by three points. But the trial cannot show this. The same average would result if a small minority benefited a great deal and everyone else not at all, or if many benefited modestly while a few were harmed. An average is a summary of a distribution, and very different distributions share the same summary. Even afterwards the matter stays hidden: a patient who takes the drug and has no stroke cannot tell whether the drug or good fortune spared him. To promise a particular patient a reduction of three points is to claim knowledge the trial does not contain.

The second error starts from this observation and draws the wrong conclusion. Since every patient is different, it says, trial results do not apply to the person in front of me, and I must rely on my clinical judgement. The premise is true and the conclusion does not follow. That patients differ is not news; what matters is whether they differ in ways that change how they respond to this treatment, and the clinician's impression is a poor instrument for discovering that. A doctor's experience is itself a kind of trial, but one without randomisation, with a small sample, no comparison group and a memory that favours vivid cases. If a large trial cannot reveal who benefits, a recollection of a few dozen patients is unlikely to do better.

Nor is the obvious remedy, examining subgroups within the trial, as reliable as it appears. Divide a trial's patients by age, sex, severity and a dozen other features, and some subgroups will show striking benefit or none at all purely by chance; the more divisions are made, the more such mirages appear. Findings of this kind have often failed to reappear when tested again. This does not mean that genuine differences in response do not exist. It means that claims about them need evidence as demanding as the evidence for the average itself, such as a plausible mechanism together with a difference that recurs in a fresh trial.

What follows is neither the tyranny of the average nor the licence of intuition. The average is the best default available when nothing more is known, and departures from it should be justified by reasons rather than by a sense that this patient is special. For some chronic conditions whose symptoms come and go quickly, it is even possible to run a trial within a single patient, alternating the treatment with a placebo over several periods and comparing the results. Such designs are not always practical, but they show what an answer to the individual question would actually require, and how little the bare assertion of individuality provides.

passage: A familiar answer to the question of why citizens owe obedience to their state is that they have agreed to it. Few of us, of course, ever signed anything, so the agreement is said to be tacit: by continuing to live within a country's borders, using its roads and accepting the protection of its courts, a person signals consent to its authority. The view is attractive because it seems to reconcile two things that are otherwise difficult to hold together, allowing us to say that political authority is genuinely binding while also maintaining that no one is bound against their will, since anyone who objects remains free to leave.

The trouble lies in that word 'free'. We do not normally count a choice as consent unless the person had a real alternative that could be taken at a bearable cost. Imagine a mining town with a single employer that also owns every shop, and suppose the company announces that anyone who keeps buying bread at its counters has thereby accepted all of its rules. No one would treat the purchase of bread as agreement, because the only way to refuse is to give up eating or to give up the town. Leaving a country is usually costlier still: it can mean abandoning one's language, one's family, one's work and the only place one knows well. There is, moreover, a further difficulty: almost every habitable stretch of the earth is now claimed by some state, so the emigrant does not escape political authority at all. She merely exchanges one authority for another, if another will admit her. The option on offer is not freedom from rule but the choice of a ruler.

Defenders of the view have a reasonable reply. Consent, they say, comes in degrees, and the availability of exit is not nothing. A state that lets its citizens leave, and lets them take their savings with them, really does treat them differently from one that seals its borders, and it seems right to say that the first has a stronger claim on their loyalty. This should be granted. A right of exit is a genuine good, and a state that denies it has failed one important test of legitimacy.

But to grant this is not to rescue the theory. That free exit is a condition of legitimacy does not make it the source of legitimacy, any more than an unlocked door makes a house a home. If a state's authority over those who stay can be justified, the justification must come from what the state does for and to them: whether its laws are fairly made, whether its burdens are fairly shared, whether its protection is extended to all. The language of tacit consent tends to obscure this question, since it allows a state to take credit for the mere fact that people have not fled, and to treat the absence of an escape as though it were an act of agreement.
